name: Kharad Compact
summary: A league of rich city-states, merchant houses and banks held together by treaties, credit and reputation rather than a crown, whose people want to know what is being promised, who bears the cost and whether the deal is fair enough to last.
government: A league of city-states, merchant houses, banks and treaty networks, coordinated by the Concordat Assembly, which sets standards and arbitrates rather than commands.
knownFor: Banking, insurance and letters of credit, patient negotiation, formal masks, dense market cities, and the Glass Compass Crash.
gateAttitude: Kharad sees the Gate era as a new world of value, risk, credit and exchange.
beliefs:
The Compact follows the **Covenant of the One**, a strict monotheism entirely separate from the First Light. The One is beyond any image, so Kharadi sacred art uses calligraphy, geometry, light and water instead. Everything else is created, and **power does not equal divinity**, a teaching that has become very useful since the Gates opened.

The heart of it is **Measure**: one word for honest weights, contracts, law and morality, and the overlap is deliberate. The great principle is *do not make two measures where the One gave one*: the rule mustn't change depending on who stands before it, though judges still weigh intention, coercion and circumstance. Vesperians ask *who wrote the principles?*; Kharadis answer that they were discovered, not invented, and the two often reach the same verdict by different roads. Wealth and power are **entrusted**, never proof of divine favour, and the successful owe the **Share of Mercy**, a charitable duty that pays for wells, hospitals, travellers and, now and then, an anonymous debtor's debt.

The One sent mortal **Messengers**, never to be worshipped. The greatest is **Nahira the Witness**, who rejected divine kingship and the sale of forgiveness. On the **Night of Broken Idols** she refused to burn incense to a king's golden ancestors: *"Your ancestors were powerful. So is a storm."* The Covenant also honours **Qorvan**, or Corven of the Honest Measure, as a mortal Messenger; Aurelia's Crowned Sun honours the same Corven as a Lantern-Bearer, and each side thinks the other badly wrong. His saying hangs in counting-houses: *a dishonest scale first cheats its owner.* The scripture is the **Recitation**, and a lot of Kharadi law grew out of arguing over it. After death comes the **Final Account**, described in commercial language that no serious teacher takes as a literal ledger.

Folklore adds the **Unseen Peoples**, neither angels nor demons, tied to ruins, wells and strange bargains, and most Kharadis are content to be polite: pour water by a dry well, and don't count your money aloud after sunset.

For the Gates the answer is short: **if it exists, it was created**. That gives Kharadi Expeditioners firm ground when something beyond a Gate claims to be a god. A chaplain's briefing: *"Be polite. Be careful. Do not kneel."* Two questions stay open: whether some Gate beings belong among the Unseen Peoples, and ownership, since *being able to reach something doesn't prove you own it*.
history:
Kharadi cities grew wherever movement gathered: river crossings, caravan routes, mountain passes, harbours. They got rich by connecting other places, and their power never rested on territory. It rested on controlling **movement, credit, storage, insurance and recognised contracts**. Foreign maps colour the Compact in one shade; Kharadis think in cities, houses and networks.

Repeated wars between the cities taught them that *a war can be expensive even when you win*, so competition moved towards tariffs, finance and arbitration. The turning point was the **Seven Tables**, rules for contracts, cross-city appeals, transferable debt, declared tariffs and cooperation against piracy, agreed after a run of ruinous trade wars. Their exact wording and date aren't settled, but they made trade between rival cities predictable enough to continue while those cities disliked each other, and Kharadis count them as the moment they became a network instead of a set of competitors.

Today the **Concordat Assembly** coordinates it all. It can't easily give orders, but it doesn't have to: a city that ignores its rulings finds its letters of credit unhonoured and its ships uninsured, and usually asks, very politely, to reopen the matter within the week. Merchant houses can own banks, shipyards and intelligence networks, and some have outlived their founding families. **Credit is trust made portable**, which is why fraud is treated so seriously: it damages every future deal. A merchant who wins every negotiation and leaves nobody willing to deal with them again is considered a fool.

The modern Compact isn't the same as every state that has ruled Kharadi lands. An older empire, the **Qadiri Ascendancy**, conquered the Old Scholastic Coast and carried out what Verna calls the **Silencing of the Schools** (see [Verna](factions.html#verna)). Many Kharadi scholars condemn it outright, often on religious grounds: the conquerors used *two measures where the One gave one*. Others argue nobody inherits unlimited liability for an empire that no longer exists. Some Kharadi institutions still hold manuscripts taken from the Coast, and whether they should go back is an open, often heated question.

**The Gates.** Auctions, salvage claims, expedition finance and insurance appeared almost as soon as the first artifacts came home. The first Kharadi question about anything from beyond a Gate is *what is this worth?*, and Kharadis are careful to separate value from price: Gate things change hands for favours, access and information as often as for coin. The lesson every apprentice hears is the **Glass Compass Crash**: an artifact from [[white-expanse|the White Expanse]] was rumoured to predict markets, a bubble formed around it, and then someone noticed it simply pointed at the nearest **refined silver**. Three merchant houses collapsed. A fourth made a great deal of money selling silver.
visualSummary:
A Kharadi city is something you learn by moving through it: covered markets, courtyards with fountains, bridges, warehouses, banks and temples, coloured glass throwing light across the stalls. Visitors get lost, get offered tea eleven times, and get walked to where they were going by a stallholder who expects to be remembered. The palette is **pale stone, turquoise, deep blue, ivory, copper, bronze, burgundy, black and gold**; the common motifs are the **scales** for justice and contracts, the **diamond** for the unity of the cities, and geometry everywhere.

Clothing is shaped by heat, travel and trade: layered, flowing garments, sashes, jewellery and patterned cloth, varying a lot from city to city. **Seals, ledgers and contract cases** travel with every merchant and envoy. **Formal masks** are worn in some negotiations, auctions and ceremonies, never in the street. A mask stands for the house, bank or office the wearer speaks for, so taking it off in the middle of a negotiation says *this has become personal*. Machinery is modular and easy to resell, and still often carries geometric trim as carefully made as a carpet.

The lazy foreign stereotype is greed. It misses nearly everything: what Kharad prizes is trust, reputation and correct measure, and a Kharadi who is only greedy is, by Kharadi standards, just bad at business.
materials: Pale stone, turquoise and deep blue, copper and bronze, patterned textiles, coloured glass and glazed ceramic

relations.text: Deeply interdependent: finance and insurance for imperial markets and naval protection.
Warm, practical trade; Kharadis find the Vardic distrust of debt sensible, if unsophisticated.
An important customer and a loud critic.
One of the oldest great trade relationships: patient negotiation on both sides.
Distant, complicated and functional, for reasons that go back to the Silencing of the Schools.

extraRule: An extra Mild Consequence slot, **Minor Obligation**: instead of paying up to 2 Coins, someone covers the cost and you record the debt. You clear it by completing a Project and offering its result to the Kharad Compact.
